t: 3177. Find the Maximum Length of a Good Subsequence II
o: A good subsequence has at most k adjacent unequal pairs. We want the longest good subsequence of nums (n up to 5000, k up to 50). For k=0 the answer is the highest frequency of any value; in example 2 that is 2 (the two 1s). For general k, extending a subsequence by an element costs one change whenever the element differs from the current last value.
k: State: dp[j][v] = length of the best good subsequence using at most j changes and ending with value v.
Transitions: extend the same value for free, or come from the global best with j-1 changes and pay one change.
Maintaining a per-j global maximum makes each element O(k) instead of O(k · distinct).

a.n: Approach 1: DP over Change Budget and Last Value
a.i: Process nums left to right. For each element x and each budget j, the best subsequence ending at x with budget j is either the previous best ending at x with budget j (append x, no change) or the global best with budget j-1 (append x, one change). Keeping best[j] = max over all ending values lets us update each element in O(k), giving O(nk) total — about 250k operations, comfortably fast.
s: Keep k+1 hash maps dp[j] (value -> best length) and an array best[j] of global maxima.
For each x, iterate j from k down to 0: candidate = max(dp[j][x] + 1, best[j-1] + 1).
Update dp[j][x] and best[j] with the candidate (descending j keeps best[j-1] stale-correct for this round).
a.t: O(n·k) — each element triggers k constant-time map updates
a.sp: O(n·k) worst case for the hash maps of ending values

w: The descending-j loop is essential: it guarantees best[j-1] reflects the state before the current element, so we never reuse the same element twice. Verify k=0 reduces to the max frequency. Follow-ups: reconstruct an actual subsequence by storing parent pointers, or handle streaming input (the algorithm already works online).
